transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in today?

Well, doctor, they told me I had to come down here because... well, because of how I've been talking lately. See, I try to explain things to people, just regular things, but my talking gets all mixed up. Like, I was at work—I clean buildings, you know, mostly mopping floors and taking out trash and making sure the doors are secure—and I was trying to explain about the keys to my supervisor. The heavy brass ones on my ring. But then, before I know it, I'm explaining about the jail, because the keys remind me of the jail, and then somehow I'm talking about the prayer rug, the one with the fringe on the edges, and then the chess pieces... the knights and the rooks, you know, how they move around the board. 

And I'm just trying to make a simple point about my job, but I'm going on and on about the prayer rug and the chess pieces, and people just stare at me. They tell me they cannot follow what I am saying. Not a single word. And it's just so frustrating, you know? Because in my head, it all makes perfect sense, the way the keys and the jail and the rug and the chess board all connect together, it's all part of the exact same thought. But when it comes out of my mouth, people just look at me like I'm speaking a completely different language. So my boss said I need to come here and get checked out because nobody can follow my sentences anymore and it's making it hard to get my shifts done right.
Have you ever felt like your thoughts are being controlled by someone else, or that you have special powers or abilities that others don't have?

Well, controlled? No, I wouldn't say someone is steering my brain like a remote control car or nothing like that. But special abilities... see, now that is exactly it. Because there are these times... and it happens, you know, it just sort of washes over me... where my mind just opens all the way up. 

It's like a bright light switches on, and suddenly I just know things. I know exactly how everything works. I mean, on paper, I'm just the guy pushing the mop, right? I empty the trash, I wipe down the elevators, I make sure the heavy doors click shut at the end of the night. But during those times, I walk through those halls and I can see every single thing they're doing wrong. I look at the maintenance, the schedules, the way the whole place breathes, and I just know, without a shadow of a doubt, that I can fix the whole building. All of it. Top to bottom. 

I feel like I could march right up to the top floor, right into the big offices with the fancy carpets that I have to spot-clean every Tuesday, and I could sit down and teach the bosses how to run it. I really could. Because they don't see it. They don't see how the pieces move, but I do. I have this... this special way of seeing things, how it all connects together. And honestly, when I get like that, I figure I could maybe become known all over town. Like, people would hear about the guy who figured out the perfect system, and they'd come from other buildings, other businesses across the city, just to ask me how to fix their problems. Because my brain just operates on this completely different, higher level than anybody else's. 

It's a real special vision. And I try to tell my supervisor this, I really try to explain how the whole operation needs to be restructured from the ground up, but like I said before, the words get all tangled up with the keys and the chess pieces, and he just looks at me blank and tells me to get back to the mop bucket. But I know what's in my head. I know what I could do if they'd just listen.

Have there been times when you believed something was real that others told you wasn’t, like thinking you were chosen for a special mission or that you could understand messages that no one else could?

Well, it's funny you ask that, because there was this whole thing with the cameras. See, in my line of work, you're always walking the halls after everyone else has gone home, just you and the hum of the vending machines and the fluorescent lights. And a few months back, I started noticing things. Little things at first. Like the way the people who work in the building—the ones who stay late, the accountants and the lawyers and whatnot—the way they would look at me. Not just a regular "hello, janitor" look, but a look like they knew something. Like they were passing a message. 

And then it was the lights in the hallways. I'd be pushing my cart down the third-floor corridor, the one with the really stubborn scuff marks by the water cooler, and the lights would flicker. But not just a random flicker, a specific pattern. Click, click, pause, click. And I knew, I just knew deep down in my bones, that they had marked me. The building people. They knew about my special vision, about how I could fix the whole place, and they were warning each other about me. They were using the lights and those little sideways glances to keep tabs on me, to say, "Watch out for him, he knows too much."

So I went to my supervisor, right? I told him, "You gotta look at the security tapes, they're signaling each other about me." And he sighed—he does this heavy sigh whenever I come to his office—and he actually pulled up the camera footage. We sat there in that tiny little security room that always smells like stale coffee and old floor wax, and we watched the tapes. He pointed at the screen and said, "Look, nothing's happening. Nobody's looking at you funny, and the lights are just old." He showed me, plain as day, that there was nothing there on the camera. 

But... well, even with him sitting right there, showing me the tape, I still felt it. I still felt absolutely sure that they had marked me. I mean, a camera can't capture a feeling, right? A camera can't see the intention behind a look or the exact rhythm of a flickering bulb. So even though he said it wasn't real, and the tape said it wasn't real, I knew what I was experiencing. I knew they were using the hallway lights and those little looks to warn each other. It's like, they can show me all the tapes in the world, but it doesn't change what I know is happening right in front of my face, you know? It's all connected, just like the keys and the chess pieces.
Have there been times when you felt extremely low, lost interest in things you usually enjoy, or felt hopeless for several days or more?

Well, low... yeah. Yeah, there's the other side of it. It's not always the bright lights and knowing how to fix the whole building, doctor. Sometimes... sometimes it all just drains right out of me. Every single drop of it, just gone. And it can last for days, a whole week even, where everything just goes dark. 

You see, on my bad days, I'll wake up in the morning, and... well, you remember I was talking about the prayer rug earlier? The one with the fringe? I'll get up and I'll do my morning prayer, because it's a routine, you know, it's what you're supposed to do. But right after that, instead of getting ready for the day, I just sit. I sit right there on the edge of the bed. The springs are a little shot on the left side, so I sort of sink into it, and I just stay there. 

And this feeling comes over me... it's like someone poured wet concrete into my bones. I feel so heavy. Just incredibly heavy, but at the exact same time, completely empty inside. Like a hollow kind of heavy, if that makes any sense. I'll look over at my closet, I'll look at my work uniform—the blue shirt with my name stitched in white on the pocket—and I'll look at the front door, and I just feel like there is absolutely no point. No point in anything. 

I'll think to myself, what is the point of even cleaning myself up? Why bother turning on the shower or brushing my teeth? There's no point in going outside. The world out there just feels completely impossible. I'll just sit on that mattress for hours. The sun comes up, the light comes through the plastic blinds and makes those little lines across the floor, and I just watch the dust floating in the air. Now, normally, at work, I see dust and I'm right there with a microfiber cloth, taking care of it. But on those bad days, sitting on the edge of that bed, I don't care. I feel like I'm just dust, too. 

My phone will ring, and I know it's my supervisor wondering why I haven't shown up to take the trash out or mop the lobby, and I just stare at the screen. I can't even lift my arm to answer it. It's just too much weight. I just feel totally hopeless, like I'm never going to be able to move again. So, yes, I do get low. Extremely low.
Have there been times when your mood was extremely elevated, you needed less sleep, or you were much more active or talkative than usual for several days or longer?

Oh, elevated. Yeah. Elevated is a good word for it. Like taking the freight elevator all the way up to the roof, you know? Because it's the exact opposite of that wet concrete feeling I was just telling you about. Sometimes... sometimes that heavy feeling just lifts right off me, and I feel so high. Just incredibly high and powerful. It's like my blood turns into pure electricity. When I get like that, I don't just walk through the halls, I strut. I feel like I own the whole building, like I'm the most important guy in the city. 

And talkative? Oh, absolutely. I get so wound up, I'll be laughing and talking loud with everyone I see. The security guards at the front desk, the night shift maintenance guys, even the folks walking out to their cars in the parking garage. I'll just be talking their ears off, my voice echoing all the way down those long marble corridors. I'll be telling them jokes, telling them my big plans, laughing at the top of my lungs. I just feel so good, so unstoppable, you know? Like I've got the whole world figured out and I just have to share it with everybody because I've got all this energy burning inside me.

But... well, there's a catch to it. Because when I'm feeling that powerful, when my brain is moving that fast and I'm on that high frequency, I have zero patience for anybody who tries to slow me down. If someone questions me, even over something tiny... man, I can snap. Like, really snap. If my supervisor comes up while I'm explaining my brilliant ideas to the security guy, and he says something stupid like, "Why are you talking so loud?" or questions why I'm doing my rounds in a different order... I just lose it. I will shout right in his face over the smallest little thing. I go from laughing and joking to just screaming, because how dare they question me when I'm operating on that level, you know? It's like they throw a wrench into my perfect machine, and I just explode on them. So yeah, I get real high up there, but people better not push my buttons when I am.

Have there been times when your mood was extremely elevated for at least a week, where you felt so good and powerful that it was noticeable to others, even if they didn’t agree with how you were acting?

A week? Oh, easily a week. Sometimes ten days, maybe more. And "powerful" doesn't even begin to cover it, doc. It's like... it's like I suddenly have the blueprint to the whole universe unrolled right in front of my eyes, and it always starts with my building. 

You know, at those times, I'll be walking the floors, looking at the structural supports and the way the foot traffic flows, and I just absolutely believe I can fix the whole building. The whole thing! Top to bottom. I see all the inefficiencies, the wasted energy, the bad scheduling that the guys in the suits completely miss. I mean, they sit up there on the top floor with their fancy degrees—degrees I never needed, by the way, since I've got real-world experience—but they don't actually *see* the building. Not like I do. They don't feel its pulse. 

So my mind starts racing, and I realize I need to teach the bosses how to run it. I really do. I'll be mapping it all out in my head while I'm buffing the terrazzo in the main lobby, thinking about exactly how I'm going to march right past my supervisor, straight into the executive boardroom, and just lay it all out for them. I'll tell them, "Look, you're wasting money on the HVAC here, you're routing the night crew all wrong there," and I just know they'd be completely blown away. They'd probably make me a high-paid consultant right on the spot. 

And it wouldn't just stop there, either. When I'm riding that high, I know for a fact that word is gonna spread. I'd probably become known all over town for my special way of seeing things. You know? Like, the city planners or the developers of those big shiny new high-rises downtown, they'd be calling my phone non-stop. They'd be telling each other, "We need the guy who fixed the plaza, we need his vision." Because it is a vision! It's a gift. 

And sure, you asked if it's noticeable to others. Of course it is! Because I can't keep it to myself. I'll be explaining my grand designs to the night watchman or drawing complex diagrams on the back of my timecards, and yeah, maybe they look at me like I'm acting strange or talking too fast. Maybe my supervisor tells me to just calm down and empty the trash. But that's just because their brains are moving in slow motion. They can't keep up with my mind. They're stuck on the ground floor, and I'm... I'm up above the clouds, seeing the whole city grid. I just have this incredible clarity, and I know exactly what I'm capable of.
Has there ever been a time when you were so high and energized that it lasted for at least a full week, even if people around you thought you were acting unusually or needed to slow down?

A week? Oh, easily a week. More than a week sometimes. And energized doesn't even... look, when that energy comes, when it really hits me, I literally cannot sit still. I mean that. It's like a motor in my chest that just won't shut off and nobody can find the switch. 

I'll finish my regular shift, but I can't clock out and go home. I just can't go sit in my quiet apartment. So I'll go right back up to the third floor—the east wing, where the accounting department is, where they have that cheap tile that scuffs up if you even look at it wrong—and I will clean the exact same hallway over and over again. I'll sweep it, I'll mop it, I'll run the high-speed buffer over it, and then I'll get to the end of the hall, turn around, and think, "No, the shine isn't perfectly even," and I'll start the whole process all over again. Three, four, five times on the exact same stretch of floor. 

And then I'll go into their big conference rooms and start moving all the heavy leather chairs around. I'll completely rearrange them, lining up the wheels perfectly with the seams in the carpet, measuring the distance between the armrests, because nobody else sees how out of balance the room is. They just leave them pushed out every which way, and it disrupts the whole flow of the building. So I fix it. 

While I'm doing that, my brain is going so fast I have to stop and make lists. I'll grab scrap paper out of the office recycling bins—memos, old envelopes, whatever I can find—and just write page after page of lists. Inventory lists, lists of structural repairs the building needs, lists of ideas I'm going to present to the executives when they finally realize who they've got working for them. My uniform pockets will be absolutely stuffed with these lists, just bulging with paper. 

And I just keep walking. Up and down the stairwells, floor after floor, pacing the whole perimeter of the building, checking every door, every window. And the crazy thing is, my feet will be absolutely killing me. I wear these heavy work boots, you know, thick soles, steel toes, and after fourteen, sixteen hours of non-stop moving, my arches are cramping, my heels feel like they're bruised right down to the bone, I'll have blisters forming... I'll be practically limping. But I just keep walking anyway. I can't stop. Even when my feet hurt so bad it makes my eyes water, that energy just pushes me and pushes me, and I just keep going and going, day after day.

Have there been times when you felt so high or powerful that you did things that were risky, impulsive, or had serious consequences, like spending sprees, reckless driving, or aggressive confrontations?

Risky? No, no, see, that's where you're getting the wrong idea about how my mind works when I'm up there. You say impulsive, like I'm out of control, but it's the exact opposite. I am completely, one-hundred-percent dialed in. 

Take the spending sprees thing you just mentioned. I don't even know what I would buy if I wanted to! I mean, I live a very simple life. I get my check on the 15th and the 30th from the property management company—they do direct deposit now, which is fine, but it used to be paper checks and I'd have to walk down to the credit union on 4th Street before they closed at five, which was always a rush and a half. But anyway, I don't go out buying fancy clothes or big TVs or whatever people do when they lose their heads. The only thing I might spend a little of my own money on when I'm feeling that energized is... well, maybe some better cleaning supplies. Like, I'll take the bus out to the industrial supply warehouse on County Road 9, and I'll buy my own high-grade brass polish. The stuff the building provides is cheap, it leaves this awful cloudy residue, and when I'm seeing the building's true potential, I just can't stand looking at a cloudy elevator button. So I'll spend, what, twelve bucks? Fifteen? That's hardly a spree. I'm very careful with my budget. I map my expenses all out on the back of my utility bills every month.

And reckless driving? Doc, I don't even drive most of the time, but when I do, I'm driving my old '04 Malibu. It's got this terrible rattle in the front left suspension, sounds like a coffee can full of rocks if you take it over forty miles an hour. If I drove that thing recklessly, the whole front axle would probably drop right out from under me. When I drive, I take the exact same route every single time. Down Miller Avenue, left at the light by the old diner—the one that closed down last year, with the boarded-up windows—and then straight into the employee garage. Level C, spot 42. Always spot 42 because it's right next to the service elevator and I can get straight to my supply closet without dealing with the main lobby traffic. I'm precise. Every movement is calculated. I'm not reckless. 

And look, I know I said earlier that I yell at people if they get in my way, like my supervisor. But that's not... I'm not starting fistfights or getting the cops called on me or anything crazy like that. I'm not throwing punches or breaking windows. I'm just projecting my voice so they understand the absolute gravity of the situation. I have to be loud to break through their thick skulls, you know? It's not me losing control or acting impulsive, it's me trying to establish order in a place that's falling apart because nobody else pays attention. So no, I don't do anything risky that's gonna ruin my life or put me in danger. I don't have time for that nonsense. I'm too busy focusing on the work.
Have you ever had a period of time when you felt extremely low, hopeless, or lost interest in almost everything for two weeks or more in a row?

Two weeks? Doc, try a month. Sometimes longer. It's... it's like a pendulum, you know? I was just telling you about how high up I get, how I'm running on that endless motor and seeing the whole grid of the city. But then, eventually, the motor just... dies. The power gets cut. And the crash is just devastating. 

It's not just feeling a little sad or having a bad afternoon. It's physical. On my bad days, the alarm will go off at 4:15 AM, same as always, because my body is so used to the shift work. I'll roll over, and I'll do my morning prayer—I always do my morning prayer, it's a habit I've kept since I was a teenager, back before I left high school to start working. But then... after I say the words, I don't get up. I just sit there on the edge of the bed feeling incredibly heavy and empty. 

It's like I'm made of lead, but completely hollow on the inside, if that makes any sense. I'll look over at my work boots, the same ones I was just walking sixteen hours a day in, and I'll just stare at the laces. And I'll feel like there is no point in even cleaning myself up or going outside. None at all. Why bother showering? Why bother putting on the uniform? The building doesn't matter anymore. The terrazzo floors don't matter. The executives and their messy conference rooms, none of it means a single thing. 

The whole world just turns gray, like dirty mop water, and I can't find a single reason to care about any of it. I'll just sit on that mattress for hours, watching the light change in the room, feeling that heaviness pressing down on my shoulders, just completely paralyzed by how pointless everything is. And that feeling, that emptiness... it doesn't just pack up and leave after a few days. It moves in. It unpacks its bags and it stays for weeks on end.

Have there been times when you felt that other people were right to question your thoughts or actions, or did you always feel completely certain that your ideas and perceptions were correct, even when others didn’t agree with you?

Right to question me? No. No, see, that's the thing—they don't see what I see. They aren't paying attention to the details. I am completely certain, one hundred percent certain, because I'm the one actually out there in the halls day in and day out. 

Like... okay, take my supervisor. A few months ago, he actually pulled me into the main security office. It's down on the ground floor, room 112, right next to the freight elevator where it always smells like damp cardboard and that industrial pine cleaner we stopped using three years ago. Anyway, he sits me down in front of the main desk with all those monitors, and he pulls up the digital playback from the third-floor cameras. He's trying to prove to me that I was getting worked up over nothing. He's pointing at the screen, tapping his pen on the glass, saying, "Look right here, nobody is doing anything, nobody is paying any attention to you." 

And sure, on a grainy, choppy security feed, maybe it just looks like regular people walking to the bathroom or the copy machine. But a camera doesn't catch the reality of the situation. It doesn't catch the... the actual communication happening. I knew—I felt it in my gut, and I knew for an absolute fact—that the building people had marked me. The office workers, the managers, the ones who leave their half-empty coffee cups on the window sills for me to deal with. They had marked me. 

I'd be walking down the main corridor pushing my utility cart, and the hallway lights would start acting up. They have these overhead fluorescents on motion sensors that are supposed to click on when you walk by, but they were manipulating them. They were using the lights to signal each other. A flicker here, a delay there, leaving one section dark while I walked through it... it was a warning system. They were tracking me. And the looks! My supervisor couldn't see the looks on his little flat-screen monitor, but I saw them. These tiny, quick little looks they'd give each other over their cubicle walls or when they passed in the hall. Just a little dart of the eyes, a slight nod, a smirk. They were warning each other about me. 

So, no, I didn't think he was right to question me. Even when he sat there and showed me that tape and told me nothing was on the camera, it didn't change a single thing. I know what I saw. I know what they were doing with those lights and those little looks, no matter what some cheap security camera says. I was completely certain.
Have there been times when you felt your abilities or importance were so great that you believed you were destined for something extraordinary or had a special mission that others did not understand?

Extraordinary? Well, I wouldn't use that exact word, maybe, but... yes. Yes, I do. But it's not like I think I'm a prophet from the Bible or some guy in a cape on TV, it's... it's about the work. It always comes back to the work, Doc. 

When I'm dialed in, when that motor is running and I'm seeing the grid like I told you about, I can see every single flaw in that building. Not just the smudges on the glass or the scuff marks on the baseboards, but the whole... the whole ecosystem of the place. The hum of the HVAC system, the way the elevator cables tension, the flow of the foot traffic in the lobby. And I know, without a shadow of a doubt, that I can fix the whole building. All fourteen floors of it. I'm the only one who really understands how it breathes, you know? 

And the bosses? The property managers? They sit up there in their glass offices on the top floor, drinking their bottled water, looking at spreadsheets all day, but they don't know a damn thing about how to actually run a facility. They are completely clueless. When I'm in that zone, I know I could march right into their big boardroom, pull up a leather chair, and teach the bosses exactly how to run it. I could map it all out for them on their fancy whiteboards. I'd show them where they're losing efficiency, how the maintenance schedules are completely backward, how they're just putting bandaids on a failing system. 

And the thing is, I know that if they just listened to me, if they just let me take the reins and do what needs to be done, it wouldn't just stop at our building. No, word would get around. The other management companies—over at the First National tower, the big corporate parks out on the west side by the highway—they'd hear about what I did. I'd become known all over town for my special way of seeing things. People would be calling me, asking me to come look at their buildings, because nobody else has the vision I have. Nobody else pays attention to the details. So yeah, I guess you could call that a special mission. It's just... it's just so incredibly clear to me when I'm operating at that level. I know exactly what I'm capable of.
Have you ever believed, even for a short time, that you had a special connection to a higher power, the government, or some secret organization that others were unaware of?

The government? A secret organization? No. No, Doc, nothing like that. I mean, I do my morning prayers, just the regular ones my grandmother taught me back before I dropped out in the tenth grade to start pushing a broom, but I don't hear God talking back to me or giving me secret codes or anything. 

And the government? Please. I pay my taxes, well, when I'm working steady anyway, but I don't have any... any ideas about the FBI or the CIA or whoever hiding in the air ducts. I know every inch of those air ducts, especially on the seventh floor, the ones they updated back in 2018 with the new HEPA filters because the legal department complained about the air quality. I clean those vents myself, and there's nobody in there but dust mites and dead spiders. 

I really don't have the time or the energy for secret societies. The only people I deal with are the people in my building, the property managers, the office workers... the ones playing those games with the lights like I was just telling you about. But they aren't some grand secret government thing. They aren't spies. They're just middle management folks with too much time on their hands, sitting in their fabric-lined cubicles ordering those expensive twelve-dollar salads for lunch and leaving the plastic containers in the blue bins even though there's a big, bright yellow sticker that says "Paper Only" right there on the lid. I mean, it is right there. You'd think people with expensive college degrees could read a simple sign, right? But they just toss it in, dressing and all, and who has to fish it out? Me. 

So, no, it's just regular people, Doc. Not the president or the Illuminati or anything crazy like that. Just me, the mop, the building, and the people who don't respect the work. I don't need any special connection to a higher power to see what's going on right in front of my face.

Have there been times when you were absolutely certain that you had a unique and powerful ability to understand or control things that others could not, even when people close to you said it wasn’t true?

Control things? Like, what, like moving objects with my mind or making the rain stop? No, Doc, no. I mean, if I could control things, my job would be a heck of a lot easier, let me tell you. I can't even control the Clarke 20-inch industrial floor buffer when the left caster wheel gets jammed up with grit. It's this heavy, metal beast of a machine, must weigh a hundred and fifty pounds easily, and when that wheel sticks, it just pulls you right into the drywall. If I had some kind of unique power to control things, I'd just stand there with my arms crossed and make the buffer run itself up and down the main lobby, getting that perfect shine on the terrazzo without breaking a sweat. 

But no, I don't control anything. Like I was saying before, I *understand* things. I see the grid, I see how the whole building breathes and how the systems connect—the HVAC, the elevators, the foot traffic. I have that clarity. But understanding a thing isn't the same as controlling it. I can't make the plumbing on the fourth floor stop backing up, for instance. Every month, regular as clockwork, the pipes in the women's restroom over by the accounting department get clogged because they keep flushing those thick, brown, multi-fold paper towels. I put up signs. I literally taped a laminated sign right over the flush handle that says "Toilet Paper Only" in big bold letters, but do they listen? I can't control them. I can't control the pipes. I just have to go in there with the heavy-duty auger and clear it out while they all complain about the smell. 

So, no, I've never thought I had some powerful ability to control things. And nobody ever had to sit me down and tell me it wasn't true, because I never claimed it. I mean, my ex-wife, Brenda, she used to say I acted like I ruled the universe just because I wouldn't let her touch the thermostat in our apartment, but that's just because I like it at exactly 68 degrees so the compressor doesn't overwork, not because I thought I had superpowers. I just know what I know. I see the details other people miss. But control? No, I'm just the guy cleaning up the mess they leave behind.
Have there been times when you were completely certain that you had a level of importance, knowledge, or ability that was far above other people, even when they tried to tell you otherwise?

Well, yeah, Doc, that's... that's pretty much exactly what I was telling you earlier. It's like we're mopping the same floor twice here, you know? Like I said right at the start, when my motor is running like that and I'm seeing the grid, my knowledge isn't just a little better than theirs, it's... it's leaps and bounds above the rest of them. That's exactly when I know I can fix the whole building. The whole thing, top to bottom, all the systems. And I know I could march up to the top floor and teach the bosses how to actually run their own property, because they haven't got a clue how it all connects. 

And people do try to tell me otherwise. Oh, all the time. My shift supervisor, Frank, he's this guy who's been riding a desk in the basement for ten years and couldn't tell you the difference between a neutral pH floor cleaner and a heavy-duty degreaser... he'll look at me when I'm trying to explain the airflow problems in the lobby and he'll say, "Just empty the trash, man, you're not the chief engineer." Or Brenda, back when we were together, she'd say I was getting too big for my britches. She'd remind me I was just a guy who left school in the tenth grade, telling me I need to come back down to earth and stop talking crazy. 

But they don't see what I see. They don't understand that if I just had the chance to prove it, I'd be known all over town for my special way of seeing things. The other management companies would be begging for me to come look at their setups. People look at the blue uniform and the supply cart, and they think that's all I am. They try to tell me I'm just a cleaner and I don't know anything about facilities management. But when I'm in that headspace, I know for an absolute fact that my ability is lightyears ahead of theirs, no matter how many times Frank tells me to just stick to my mop. It's frustrating, Doc, it really is, when you have all the answers and everyone around you is just too blind to see it.

inference_history.note: The patient presents with disorganized speech, where thoughts are connected in a way that makes sense internally but is incomprehensible to others. This could indicate a thought disorder, such as that seen in schizophrenia (F20.9) or schizoaffective disorder (F25.9). Bipolar disorder (F31.9 and its subtypes) is also considered due to potential mood episodes accompanied by psychotic features, including disorganized thinking during manic or depressive phases. No other major symptoms are yet reported to rule out or narrow further.

patient.answer:
Well, it's funny you ask that, because there was this whole thing with the cameras. See, in my line of work, you're always walking the halls after everyone else has gone home, just you and the hum of the vending machines and the fluorescent lights. And a few months back, I started noticing things. Little things at first. Like the way the people who work in the building—the ones who stay late, the accountants and the lawyers and whatnot—the way they would look at me. Not just a regular "hello, janitor" look, but a look like they knew something. Like they were passing a message. 

And then it was the lights in the hallways. I'd be pushing my cart down the third-floor corridor, the one with the really stubborn scuff marks by the water cooler, and the lights would flicker. But not just a random flicker, a specific pattern. Click, click, pause, click. And I knew, I just knew deep down in my bones, that they had marked me. The building people. They knew about my special vision, about how I could fix the whole place, and they were warning each other about me. They were using the lights and those little sideways glances to keep tabs on me, to say, "Watch out for him, he knows too much."

So I went to my supervisor, right? I told him, "You gotta look at the security tapes, they're signaling each other about me." And he sighed—he does this heavy sigh whenever I come to his office—and he actually pulled up the camera footage. We sat there in that tiny little security room that always smells like stale coffee and old floor wax, and we watched the tapes. He pointed at the screen and said, "Look, nothing's happening. Nobody's looking at you funny, and the lights are just old." He showed me, plain as day, that there was nothing there on the camera. 

But... well, even with him sitting right there, showing me the tape, I still felt it. I still felt absolutely sure that they had marked me. I mean, a camera can't capture a feeling, right? A camera can't see the intention behind a look or the exact rhythm of a flickering bulb. So even though he said it wasn't real, and the tape said it wasn't real, I knew what I was experiencing. I knew they were using the hallway lights and those little looks to warn each other. It's like, they can show me all the tapes in the world, but it doesn't change what I know is happening right in front of my face, you know? It's all connected, just like the keys and the chess pieces.

Well, low... yeah. Yeah, there's the other side of it. It's not always the bright lights and knowing how to fix the whole building, doctor. Sometimes... sometimes it all just drains right out of me. Every single drop of it, just gone. And it can last for days, a whole week even, where everything just goes dark. 

You see, on my bad days, I'll wake up in the morning, and... well, you remember I was talking about the prayer rug earlier? The one with the fringe? I'll get up and I'll do my morning prayer, because it's a routine, you know, it's what you're supposed to do. But right after that, instead of getting ready for the day, I just sit. I sit right there on the edge of the bed. The springs are a little shot on the left side, so I sort of sink into it, and I just stay there. 

And this feeling comes over me... it's like someone poured wet concrete into my bones. I feel so heavy. Just incredibly heavy, but at the exact same time, completely empty inside. Like a hollow kind of heavy, if that makes any sense. I'll look over at my closet, I'll look at my work uniform—the blue shirt with my name stitched in white on the pocket—and I'll look at the front door, and I just feel like there is absolutely no point. No point in anything. 

I'll think to myself, what is the point of even cleaning myself up? Why bother turning on the shower or brushing my teeth? There's no point in going outside. The world out there just feels completely impossible. I'll just sit on that mattress for hours. The sun comes up, the light comes through the plastic blinds and makes those little lines across the floor, and I just watch the dust floating in the air. Now, normally, at work, I see dust and I'm right there with a microfiber cloth, taking care of it. But on those bad days, sitting on the edge of that bed, I don't care. I feel like I'm just dust, too. 

My phone will ring, and I know it's my supervisor wondering why I haven't shown up to take the trash out or mop the lobby, and I just stare at the screen. I can't even lift my arm to answer it. It's just too much weight. I just feel totally hopeless, like I'm never going to be able to move again. So, yes, I do get low. Extremely low.

Oh, elevated. Yeah. Elevated is a good word for it. Like taking the freight elevator all the way up to the roof, you know? Risky? No, no, see, that's where you're getting the wrong idea about how my mind works when I'm up there. You say impulsive, like I'm out of control, but it's the exact opposite. I am completely, one-hundred-percent dialed in. 

Take the spending sprees thing you just mentioned. I don't even know what I would buy if I wanted to! I mean, I live a very simple life. I get my check on the 15th and the 30th from the property management company—they do direct deposit now, which is fine, but it used to be paper checks and I'd have to walk down to the credit union on 4th Street before they closed at five, which was always a rush and a half. But anyway, I don't go out buying fancy clothes or big TVs or whatever people do when they lose their heads. The only thing I might spend a little of my own money on when I'm feeling that energized is... well, maybe some better cleaning supplies. It's got this terrible rattle in the front left suspension, sounds like a coffee can full of rocks if you take it over forty miles an hour. I'm not reckless. 

And look, I know I said earlier that I yell at people if they get in my way, like my supervisor. But that's not... I'm not starting fistfights or getting the cops called on me or anything crazy like that. I'm not throwing punches or breaking windows. I'm just projecting my voice so they understand the absolute gravity of the situation. I have to be loud to break through their thick skulls, you know? It's not me losing control or acting impulsive, it's me trying to establish order in a place that's falling apart because nobody else pays attention. So no, I don't do anything risky that's gonna ruin my life or put me in danger. I don't have time for that nonsense. I'm too busy focusing on the work.

The terrazzo floors don't matter. The executives and their messy conference rooms, none of it means a single thing. 

The whole world just turns gray, like dirty mop water, and I can't find a single reason to care about any of it. I'll just sit on that mattress for hours, watching the light change in the room, feeling that heaviness pressing down on my shoulders, just completely paralyzed by how pointless everything is. patient.answer:
Right to question me? No. No, see, that's the thing—they don't see what I see. They aren't paying attention to the details. I am completely certain, one hundred percent certain, because I'm the one actually out there in the halls day in and day out. 

Like... okay, take my supervisor. A few months ago, he actually pulled me into the main security office. It's down on the ground floor, room 112, right next to the freight elevator where it always smells like damp cardboard and that industrial pine cleaner we stopped using three years ago. Anyway, he sits me down in front of the main desk with all those monitors, and he pulls up the digital playback from the third-floor cameras. He's trying to prove to me that I was getting worked up over nothing. He's pointing at the screen, tapping his pen on the glass, saying, "Look right here, nobody is doing anything, nobody is paying any attention to you." 

And sure, on a grainy, choppy security feed, maybe it just looks like regular people walking to the bathroom or the copy machine. But a camera doesn't catch the reality of the situation. It doesn't catch the... the actual communication happening. I knew—I felt it in my gut, and I knew for an absolute fact—that the building people had marked me. The office workers, the managers, the ones who leave their half-empty coffee cups on the window sills for me to deal with. They had marked me. 

I'd be walking down the main corridor pushing my utility cart, and the hallway lights would start acting up. They have these overhead fluorescents on motion sensors that are supposed to click on when you walk by, but they were manipulating them. They were using the lights to signal each other. A flicker here, a delay there, leaving one section dark while I walked through it... it was a warning system. They were tracking me. And the looks! My supervisor couldn't see the looks on his little flat-screen monitor, but I saw them. These tiny, quick little looks they'd give each other over their cubicle walls or when they passed in the hall. Just a little dart of the eyes, a slight nod, a smirk. They were warning each other about me. 

So, no, I didn't think he was right to question me. Even when he sat there and showed me that tape and told me nothing was on the camera, it didn't change a single thing. I know what I saw. I know what they were doing with those lights and those little looks, no matter what some cheap security camera says. I was completely certain.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a manic episode that included inflated self-esteem or grandiosity, which is key to differentiating between F31.9 (Bipolar Disorder) and F25.9 (Schizoaffective Disorder).
doctor.question: Have there been times when you felt your abilities or importance were so great that you believed you were destined for something extraordinary or had a special mission that others did not understand?

target_item.name: Inflated_Self_Esteem
target_item.manifestation: At those times I believe I can fix the whole building, teach the bosses how to run it, and maybe become known all over town for my special way of seeing things.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question asks if the patient felt their abilities or importance were so great that they believed they were destined for something extraordinary or had a special mission. This directly addresses inflated self-esteem or grandiosity, which matches the S035 symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Extraordinary? Well, I wouldn't use that exact word, maybe, but... yes. Yes, I do. But it's not like I think I'm a prophet from the Bible or some guy in a cape on TV, it's... it's about the work. It always comes back to the work, Doc. 

When I'm dialed in, when that motor is running and I'm seeing the grid like I told you about, I can see every single flaw in that building. Not just the smudges on the glass or the scuff marks on the baseboards, but the whole... the whole ecosystem of the place. The hum of the HVAC system, the way the elevator cables tension, the flow of the foot traffic in the lobby. And I know, without a shadow of a doubt, that I can fix the whole building. All fourteen floors of it. I'm the only one who really understands how it breathes, you know? 

And the bosses? The property managers? They sit up there in their glass offices on the top floor, drinking their bottled water, looking at spreadsheets all day, but they don't know a damn thing about how to actually run a facility. They are completely clueless. When I'm in that zone, I know I could march right into their big boardroom, pull up a leather chair, and teach the bosses exactly how to run it. I could map it all out for them on their fancy whiteboards. I'd show them where they're losing efficiency, how the maintenance schedules are completely backward, how they're just putting bandaids on a failing system. 

And the thing is, I know that if they just listened to me, if they just let me take the reins and do what needs to be done, it wouldn't just stop at our building. No, word would get around. The other management companies—over at the First National tower, the big corporate parks out on the west side by the highway—they'd hear about what I did. I'd become known all over town for my special way of seeing things. People would be calling me, asking me to come look at their buildings, because nobody else has the vision I have. Nobody else pays attention to the details. So yeah, I guess you could call that a special mission. It's just... it's just so incredibly clear to me when I'm operating at that level. I know exactly what I'm capable of.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced delusions of grandeur, a key symptom of schizophrenia (F25.9), which would help distinguish it from bipolar disorder (F31.9).
doctor.question: Have you ever believed, even for a short time, that you had a special connection to a higher power, the government, or some secret organization that others were unaware of?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about delusions involving a special connection to a higher power, the government, or a secret organization. The patient's profile includes delusions about being marked by building staff (S019) and grandiosity about fixing buildings (S035), but no beliefs regarding higher powers, government, or secret organizations.

patient.answer:
The government? A secret organization? No. No, Doc, nothing like that. I mean, I do my morning prayers, just the regular ones my grandmother taught me back before I dropped out in the tenth grade to start pushing a broom, but I don't hear God talking back to me or giving me secret codes or anything. 

And the government? Please. I pay my taxes, well, when I'm working steady anyway, but I don't have any... any ideas about the FBI or the CIA or whoever hiding in the air ducts. I know every inch of those air ducts, especially on the seventh floor, the ones they updated back in 2018 with the new HEPA filters because the legal department complained about the air quality. I clean those vents myself, and there's nobody in there but dust mites and dead spiders. 

I really don't have the time or the energy for secret societies. The only people I deal with are the people in my building, the property managers, the office workers... the ones playing those games with the lights like I was just telling you about. But they aren't some grand secret government thing. They aren't spies. They're just middle management folks with too much time on their hands, sitting in their fabric-lined cubicles ordering those expensive twelve-dollar salads for lunch and leaving the plastic containers in the blue bins even though there's a big, bright yellow sticker that says "Paper Only" right there on the lid. I mean, it is right there. You'd think people with expensive college degrees could read a simple sign, right? But they just toss it in, dressing and all, and who has to fish it out? Me. 

So, no, it's just regular people, Doc. Not the president or the Illuminati or anything crazy like that. Just me, the mop, the building, and the people who don't respect the work. I don't need any special connection to a higher power to see what's going on right in front of my face.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced delusions of grandeur that are fixed and unshakable, a key feature of bipolar disorder with psychotic features (F25.9), as opposed to bipolar disorder without psychotic features (F31.9).
doctor.question: Have there been times when you were absolutely certain that you had a unique and powerful ability to understand or control things that others could not, even when people close to you said it wasn’t true?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about delusions of grandiosity or control (having a unique and powerful ability to understand or control things). The patient's profile does not include this specific type of delusion, and their inflated self-esteem has already been addressed.

patient.answer:
Control things? Like, what, like moving objects with my mind or making the rain stop? No, Doc, no. I mean, if I could control things, my job would be a heck of a lot easier, let me tell you. I can't even control the Clarke 20-inch industrial floor buffer when the left caster wheel gets jammed up with grit. It's this heavy, metal beast of a machine, must weigh a hundred and fifty pounds easily, and when that wheel sticks, it just pulls you right into the drywall. If I had some kind of unique power to control things, I'd just stand there with my arms crossed and make the buffer run itself up and down the main lobby, getting that perfect shine on the terrazzo without breaking a sweat. 

But no, I don't control anything. Like I was saying before, I *understand* things. I see the grid, I see how the whole building breathes and how the systems connect—the HVAC, the elevators, the foot traffic. I have that clarity. But understanding a thing isn't the same as controlling it. I can't make the plumbing on the fourth floor stop backing up, for instance. Every month, regular as clockwork, the pipes in the women's restroom over by the accounting department get clogged because they keep flushing those thick, brown, multi-fold paper towels. I put up signs. I literally taped a laminated sign right over the flush handle that says "Toilet Paper Only" in big bold letters, but do they listen? I can't control them. I can't control the pipes. I just have to go in there with the heavy-duty auger and clear it out while they all complain about the smell. 

So, no, I've never thought I had some powerful ability to control things. And nobody ever had to sit me down and tell me it wasn't true, because I never claimed it. I mean, my ex-wife, Brenda, she used to say I acted like I ruled the universe just because I wouldn't let her touch the thermostat in our apartment, but that's just because I like it at exactly 68 degrees so the compressor doesn't overwork, not because I thought I had superpowers. I just know what I know. I see the details other people miss. But control? No, I'm just the guy cleaning up the mess they leave behind.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced delusions of grandeur or an inflated sense of importance that is fixed and unshakable, a key feature of manic episodes in bipolar disorder and also relevant to schizophrenia.
doctor.question: Have there been times when you were completely certain that you had a level of importance, knowledge, or ability that was far above other people, even when they tried to tell you otherwise?

target_item.name: Inflated_Self_Esteem
target_item.manifestation: At those times I believe I can fix the whole building, teach the bosses how to run it, and maybe become known all over town for my special way of seeing things.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of having a level of importance, knowledge, or ability far above others, which directly corresponds to inflated self-esteem and grandiosity.

patient.answer:
Well, yeah, Doc, that's... that's pretty much exactly what I was telling you earlier. It's like we're mopping the same floor twice here, you know? Like I said right at the start, when my motor is running like that and I'm seeing the grid, my knowledge isn't just a little better than theirs, it's... it's leaps and bounds above the rest of them. That's exactly when I know I can fix the whole building. The whole thing, top to bottom, all the systems. And I know I could march up to the top floor and teach the bosses how to actually run their own property, because they haven't got a clue how it all connects. 

And people do try to tell me otherwise. Oh, all the time. My shift supervisor, Frank, he's this guy who's been riding a desk in the basement for ten years and couldn't tell you the difference between a neutral pH floor cleaner and a heavy-duty degreaser... he'll look at me when I'm trying to explain the airflow problems in the lobby and he'll say, "Just empty the trash, man, you're not the chief engineer." Or Brenda, back when we were together, she'd say I was getting too big for my britches. She'd remind me I was just a guy who left school in the tenth grade, telling me I need to come back down to earth and stop talking crazy. 

But they don't see what I see. They don't understand that if I just had the chance to prove it, I'd be known all over town for my special way of seeing things. The other management companies would be begging for me to come look at their setups. People look at the blue uniform and the supply cart, and they think that's all I am. They try to tell me I'm just a cleaner and I don't know anything about facilities management. But when I'm in that headspace, I know for an absolute fact that my ability is lightyears ahead of theirs, no matter how many times Frank tells me to just stick to my mop. It's frustrating, Doc, it really is, when you have all the answers and everyone around you is just too blind to see it.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits a clear pattern of alternating episodes of elevated mood with grandiosity, pressured speech, and hyperactivity consistent with mania, alternating with episodes of severe depression. However, the presence of persistent, non-bizarre delusions—specifically, the belief that coworkers are signaling each other about him using hallway lights and subtle glances, despite contradictory objective evidence—indicates a psychotic disorder rather than a primary mood disorder. These delusions are fixed and unshakable, and the patient remains fully convinced of their validity despite contradictory evidence. This combination of affective symptoms and non-bizarre delusions aligns with schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type (F25.9).
